note: A human-in-the-loop debiasing tool that records the reasoning behind each change, which produces the audit trail fairness work usually lacks.
title: D-BIAS: A Causality-Based Human-in-the-Loop System for Tackling Algorithmic Bias
journal: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
explain_beginner: AI systems can pick up social biases from the data they learn from, which is a problem when they are used in areas like hiring or healthcare. This paper introduces a tool called D-BIAS that lets a person examine a dataset and find unfair patterns, such as bias against women or Black women. The user can then adjust the underlying causes of bias and see how those changes affect fairness and data quality. The tool creates a new, fairer dataset while keeping it close to the original. Tests showed it reduced bias more than a standard method, with only small downsides, and people trusted it more than a fully automated approach.
explain_business: This research offers a practical way to reduce bias in AI models that use tabular data, such as those in hiring, lending, or healthcare. The D-BIAS tool lets a human expert adjust the causes of bias and immediately see the impact on fairness, accuracy, and data quality. It produces a debiased dataset that can be used for downstream tasks. Tests show it cuts bias more than a standard method while keeping data changes small and performance loss low. For executives, this means a more trustworthy, auditable path to fairer AI, which can help meet compliance goals and reduce reputational risk. The decision it informs is whether to adopt a human-in-the-loop debiasing tool instead of a fully automated one.
explain_practitioner: The paper presents D-BIAS, a visual interactive system for auditing and mitigating bias in tabular datasets. It builds a graphical causal model to encode feature relationships and allow domain knowledge injection. Users identify unfair causal edges via fairness metrics, then weaken or delete them. For each edit, a novel method simulates a debiased dataset that minimally diverges from the original while respecting the updated causal model. Users can inspect effects on fairness, utility, distortion, and distribution. Experiments on three datasets and a user study show D-BIAS reduces bias more than a baseline debiasing method, with low distortion and small utility loss, and outperforms an automated approach on trust, interpretability, and accountability.
